paras: The mutilation of George Houston was an attack on a Black hackman by a mob of about 100 masked, armed men in Tampa, Florida, on the night of July 30, 1903. The mob took Houston from a city detective who was taking him to the county jail, drove him outside the city limits, and mutilated him, but left him alive. A second masked mob shot a Black tailor the next night, and within weeks Houston had left the city.

According to a Tampa dispatch to the Savannah Morning News, two policemen discovered Houston on the morning of July 30 "improperly familiar" with Annie Groover, a white girl of fourteen. The police said they had watched the pair for two weeks and had evidence that he had been enticing her to his room for several months, describing her as "half-witted." The New York Sun's wire version instead said he had been caught "while assaulting" the girl, whom it named Annie Grooves.

That night City Detective Bell was taking Houston by carriage from the police station to the county jail by a roundabout route when about 100 masked, armed men surrounded the carriage. The mob seized and held the detective, gagged Houston, put a black cap over his head, and drove him in another carriage to the gun club grounds, "a lonely spot just outside the city limits." There he was bound and mutilated, the knife wielded by a leading member of the mob "said to be a physician"; the Sun called it "a nameless surgical operation."

The mob left Houston at the spot, and after someone told the police where he was, officers took him to the colored hospital, where he was treated to keep him from bleeding to death. Black residents were reported "considerably worked up" and gathering in their section of the city that night, though the dispatch expected no serious trouble.

On the night of July 31 another party of masked men surrounded the house of M. M. Wadkins, a Black tailor on the principal street, and tried to treat him "in the same manner." Wadkins ran, was shot in the chin and the leg, and escaped through the house of A. J. Knight onto its roof, after which police guarded him. The Savannah paper said he was suspected of "criminal intimacy with white women, the same offense" charged to Houston, and Wadkins offered a $500 reward for the arrest of his attackers.

In late August the Tampa Morning Tribune reported that Houston, released from the hospital several days earlier, had "mysteriously disappeared" and was believed to have followed Wadkins out of the city. Other Black residents, among them Thomas McKnight, had received anonymous threatening letters. No report of arrests, an investigation or a prosecution for either attack appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News carried the fullest account on July 31 under the headline "Victim of a Mob," with a subhead saying "Vengeance Was Wrought Upon a Negro Hackman," and it followed with the Wadkins attack the next day. The New York Sun's special, printed in the Minneapolis Journal, ran as "Mob Inflicts Dread Penalty," calling Houston a "Negro Assailant" who was "Terribly Punished" and saying the mob "Refuses to Kill Him, but Inflicts a Nameless Torture." Small Midwestern papers reprinted that story into August under the subhead "Nameless Operation Performed on Negro Ravisher," and a South Dakota weekly reduced it to one line in its news digest.

The New-York Tribune headlined the Wadkins attack "Chased Negro and Shot Him," adding that "He Would Not Wait to See What Florida Mob Wanted." Weeks later a Savannah Morning News item on a convict shot near Tampa said the man would suffer the fate that had made Houston "a local celebrity." No coverage of the attack was found in the Black press.

The accounts differ on the charge against Houston: the first Tampa dispatch said he was found "improperly familiar" with the girl and that she had yielded to his persuasions, while the Sun wire and its reprints said he was caught assaulting her. Both versions rest on what the police said, and no court heard the charge in the coverage.

reader.title: Mutilation of George Houston
bases: A masked mob seized Houston from an officer and mutilated him but left him alive, and one headline says the mob refused to kill him (A1, A2, A8).
The Tampa dispatches of July 30-31 (A1, A2) and the later Tampa Morning Tribune item (A8) independently report the mob's mutilation of Houston and his treatment in hospital.

accounts.label: Tampa dispatch to the Savannah Morning News
accounts.gist: Houston was found by police 'improperly familiar' with a white girl; that night 100 masked, armed men took him from Detective Bell's carriage and mutilated him at the gun club grounds.

accounts.label: New York Sun wire
accounts.gist: Houston was caught 'while assaulting' the girl and was subjected to a 'nameless surgical operation' by a mob member said to be a physician; omits the masks, the mob's size and the detective's name.

accounts.label: Police claim
accounts.gist: Police said they had watched the pair for two weeks and had evidence Houston had been enticing the girl to his room for months.

accounts.label: Tampa Morning Tribune
accounts.gist: Houston was operated on by the mob 'because of his attentions to a white girl', was released from hospital and disappeared from Tampa.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Victim of a Mob' and 'Vengeance Was Wrought Upon a Negro Hackman', but gave the police's account of the girl as fact.
The Sun wire ran as 'Mob Inflicts Dread Penalty', calling Houston a 'Negro Assailant' who was 'Terribly Punished', and in later reprints a 'Negro Ravisher'.
The New-York Tribune's headline on the Wadkins attack, 'He Would Not Wait to See What Florida Mob Wanted', treated the second attack lightly.
The Savannah Morning News's later Tampa item called Houston 'a local celebrity' made so by the mob's operation.

versions.value: Discovered 'improperly familiar' with the girl; police say he had enticed her to his room for months and she 'yielded to his persuasions'

conflicts.note: The Savannah dispatch, the fullest and earliest, does not allege assault; the Sun wire version and its reprints do. All versions come from police or press, not from a court.
Likely a transmission variant of one name.
